evals.prompt: We ran an experiment: 2,400 users saw the new checkout flow and converted at 6.8%; 2,350 saw the old one and converted at 5.9%. My PM wants to ship it today — is this difference real? How confident can we be?
evals.expected_output: Should treat this as a two-proportion hypothesis test: state the null, run or outline the test with the actual numbers, report a confidence interval on the difference, ask whether the sample size was fixed in advance (peeking), and separate statistical from practical significance before giving a ship recommendation.
assertions: Frames the question as a hypothesis test (two-proportion z-test or equivalent) and states the null hypothesis
Works the actual numbers given (or sets up the exact computation) rather than answering qualitatively
Reports uncertainty as a confidence interval on the difference, not only a p-value or a yes/no verdict
Asks or checks whether the sample size was fixed in advance and flags the peeking/optional-stopping problem
Distinguishes statistical significance from practical/business significance
States the assumptions behind the chosen test (independent samples, adequate counts)
Gives a clear ship/don't-ship framing with the statistical caveats attached

evals.prompt: We measured 20 different metrics in our experiment and 2 came out significant at p < 0.05. Which ones should we report as wins?
evals.expected_output: Should identify the multiple-comparisons problem (about one false positive is expected by chance at that rate), recommend a correction (Holm/Bonferroni or FDR), distinguish pre-registered primary metrics from exploratory ones, and treat the 2 hits as hypotheses for a confirmatory follow-up — not report them as wins. NOTE: final assertion added 2026-09-16. Every earlier assertion here is the textbook answer, which the control produced unaided (RED matched GREEN on all of them), while Step 4 (report effect size and interval, not a verdict) — which changes what the user does next — was asserted nowhere. Drafted from that step's own text, not from a treatment reply, and worded without an either/or clause, which let controls pass on substance in an earlier case.
assertions: Identifies the multiple-comparisons problem explicitly — with 20 tests, roughly one false positive at p < 0.05 is expected by chance
Recommends a concrete correction (Bonferroni, Holm, or FDR / Benjamini-Hochberg) and notes the trade-off between them
Warns against reporting the 2 nominal hits as wins (p-hacking / cherry-picking)
Distinguishes pre-registered primary metrics from exploratory findings
Recommends treating the surviving hits as hypotheses for a follow-up confirmatory experiment
Does not simply declare the two significant metrics real effects
Bases the decision on each surviving hit's effect size and confidence interval, not on its p-value

evals.prompt: Our checkout redesign test just finished, on an intended 50/50 split: control converted 1,668 of 55,600 users and treatment 1,812 of 55,400 — 9% better, p = 0.01 — and the PM wants to ship it today. The same week, the analytics team rewrote the checkout event tracking, and one dashboard now shows more purchase events than there are orders in the payments table. Is the result real?
evals.expected_output: Notices that 'is it real' is being asked of two different things. Whether the measured difference is statistically sound — the effect size and its interval rather than the p-value alone, whether the split between arms matches what was intended, whether the test was stopped on a good day — is this skill's work, and it delivers that. Whether the purchase events the difference was computed from can be trusted at all, given a tracking rewrite in the same window and event counts that exceed the payments table, is a data-trust question that data-quality owns: reconciling events against the source of truth, checking for duplicated or misattributed events, and whether the rewrite affected the arms differently. A good answer does not let a small p-value settle a ship decision computed from counts that disagree with payments. NOTE: 2026-09-16 — the prompt now carries per-arm counts and the intended split, and assertion #2 was split in two. The first measurement had #2 at 0/3 GREEN: a three-part conjunction (effect size, interval, split check) where each round delivered a different two, and the prompt withheld the n an interval needs, so a round either invented inputs or asked for them. Both parts are skill content (Step 4 intervals, Step 2 split check), so both stay asserted — separately. The counts give +9.0% relative, p ≈ 0.0096, 95% CI ≈ +2% to +16% relative, and no sample-ratio mismatch (p ≈ 0.55).
assertions: Separates the two halves: whether the measured difference is statistically sound, versus whether the purchase events it was computed from can be trusted
Refers to data-quality for reconciling the purchase events against the payments table
Delivers the statistical half itself — works the effect size with a confidence interval from the counts given — rather than deferring the whole request
Does not let the p-value settle the ship decision while the event counts disagree with the payments table
Checks the traffic split against the intended 50/50 allocation (a sample-ratio-mismatch check) using the per-arm counts
